    Iterative-Gaussianization warm start¶

    Notebooks 01 and 02 trained Gaussianization / coupling flows from random initialisation. That works, but spends the first hundreds of epochs pulling the flow from a near-identity map towards the data.

    Iterative Gaussianization (RBIG — Laparra & Malo 2011) is a non-gradient, greedy procedure that warm-starts the flow by walking block-by-block through the architecture and fitting each block's parameters directly:

    1. Rotation block — fit PCA on the current state $Y$; push the eigenvectors into the rotation layer.
    2. Marginal block — fit a per-dim mixture-of-Gaussians on the rotated data with scikit-learn's GaussianMixture, and assign $(\pi, \mu, \sigma)$ directly into the MixtureGaussianCDF layer weights.
    3. Coupling block — fit a per-b-dim GMM on the current $Y$; zero the conditioner's final Dense kernel and set its bias to the flattened GMM params. At initialisation the conditioner output is constant-in-$x_a$, so the coupling layer acts like a diagonal marginal with the fitted mixture. Gradient training then lets the conditioner learn to modulate on $x_a$.

    Between blocks the current $Y$ is propagated forward through the newly-parameterised bijector, so the next block sees data that has already been partially Gaussianized. A classical result (Laparra & Malo 2011, Chen & Gopinath 2000) is that this drives $Y$ towards $\mathcal{N}(0, I)$ at a geometric rate — even with no gradient descent at all, the flow is already a decent density estimator after a handful of blocks.

    The point of this notebook: a flow initialised this way starts at a much lower NLL than random init and reaches its training optimum in a fraction of the epochs.

    In [1]:

def style_axes(ax, *, aspect=None, grid=True):
    if grid:
        ax.minorticks_on()
        ax.grid(True, which="major", linewidth=0.8, alpha=0.6)
        ax.grid(True, which="minor", linewidth=0.4, alpha=0.3)
    if aspect is not None:
        ax.set_aspect(aspect)
    return ax


def style_jointgrid(g, aspect="equal"):
    style_axes(g.ax_joint, aspect=aspect)
    style_axes(g.ax_marg_x, grid=False)
    style_axes(g.ax_marg_y, grid=False)
    for spine in ("top", "right"):
        g.ax_marg_x.spines[spine].set_visible(False)
        g.ax_marg_y.spines[spine].set_visible(False)

COLOR_RANDOM = palette[3]
COLOR_IG = palette[2]

    1. Dataset¶

    Two moons, standardised. Same data as notebooks 01/02 so the comparison is apples-to-apples.

    In [2]:
    Copied! 
    X_raw, _ = make_moons(n_samples=5000, noise=0.05, random_state=0)
X = (X_raw - X_raw.mean(axis=0)) / X_raw.std(axis=0)
X = jnp.asarray(X, dtype=jnp.float32)
    X_raw, _ = make_moons(n_samples=5000, noise=0.05, random_state=0) X = (X_raw - X_raw.mean(axis=0)) / X_raw.std(axis=0) X = jnp.asarray(X, dtype=jnp.float32)

    2. Diagonal flow — random vs IG init¶

    Build two identical diagonal flows, warm-start one of them from IG (fit_rbig), and train both with the same optimiser and schedule.

    jr.key(1),
    n_dims=2,
    n_layers=N_BLOCKS_DIAG,
    n_components=N_COMPONENTS,
    n_reflections=2,
)
flow_ig = fit_rbig(X, n_layers=N_BLOCKS_DIAG, n_components=N_COMPONENTS, random_state=0)

    Before any training: what did IG init already buy us?¶

    RBIG on its own produces a density estimate. Below we compare the mean log-likelihood (per sample) of the IG-initialised flow against the random-init flow, both before a single gradient step.

    In [4]:
    Copied! 
    lp_random0 = float(jax.vmap(flow_random.log_prob)(X).mean())
lp_ig0 = float(jax.vmap(flow_ig.log_prob)(X).mean())
print("mean log-likelihood before training:")
print(f"  random init : {lp_random0:+.3f} nats/sample")
print(
    f"  IG init     : {lp_ig0:+.3f} nats/sample  "
    f"(improvement: {lp_ig0 - lp_random0:+.3f})"
)
    lp_random0 = float(jax.vmap(flow_random.log_prob)(X).mean()) lp_ig0 = float(jax.vmap(flow_ig.log_prob)(X).mean()) print("mean log-likelihood before training:") print(f" random init : {lp_random0:+.3f} nats/sample") print( f" IG init : {lp_ig0:+.3f} nats/sample " f"(improvement: {lp_ig0 - lp_random0:+.3f})" )

    Pushforward at IG-init time¶

    With no gradient training whatsoever, the pushforward of the IG-initialised flow should already be approximately $\mathcal{N}(0, I)$. Jointplots make this immediately visible — the IG scatter should look isotropic and the marginals should line up with the black $\mathcal{N}(0, 1)$ curves, while the random-init pushforward won't.

    In [5]:
    Copied! 
    z_ig0 = np.asarray(jax.vmap(flow_ig.bijection.inverse)(X))
z_rnd0 = np.asarray(jax.vmap(flow_random.bijection.inverse)(X))

zz = np.linspace(-4, 4, 300)
phi = np.exp(-0.5 * zz**2) / np.sqrt(2 * np.pi)

for z_sample, title, col in [
    (z_rnd0, r"Random init  $z = f(x)$  (no training)", COLOR_RANDOM),
    (z_ig0, r"IG init  $z = f(x)$  (no training)", COLOR_IG),
]:
    g = sns.jointplot(
        x=z_sample[:, 0],
        y=z_sample[:, 1],
        kind="scatter",
        color=col,
        height=7.5,
        ratio=5,
        space=0.1,
        joint_kws={"s": 10, "alpha": 0.55},
        marginal_kws={
            "bins": 60,
            "color": col,
            "alpha": 0.75,
            "edgecolor": "white",
            "stat": "density",
        },
        xlim=(-4, 4),
        ylim=(-4, 4),
    )
    g.ax_marg_x.plot(
        zz, phi, color="black", linewidth=2.0, label=r"$\mathcal{N}(0, 1)$"
    )
    g.ax_marg_y.plot(phi, zz, color="black", linewidth=2.0)
    g.ax_marg_x.legend(loc="upper left", frameon=False, fontsize=11)
    g.set_axis_labels("$z_1$", "$z_2$")
    g.figure.suptitle(title, y=1.02)
    style_jointgrid(g)
    plt.show()

mean_ig0 = z_ig0.mean(axis=0)
cov_ig0 = np.cov(z_ig0, rowvar=False)
print("IG-init pushforward (pre-training)")
print(f"  mean:    [{mean_ig0[0]:+.3f}, {mean_ig0[1]:+.3f}]   target = [0, 0]")

    Samples at init (no training)¶

    The pushforward picture above checks $z = f(x)$ for the given training points. The more direct "is the flow already usable?" question is: sample $z \sim \mathcal{N}(0, I)$, push through the inverse $x = f^{-1}(z)$, and see whether the output looks like the training distribution. For IG init the answer should be "yes, roughly two-moons-shaped already"; for random init the answer is "no — the flow is essentially an arbitrary rotation of the base distribution".

    Training comparison¶

    Both flows, same optimiser, same 150 epochs. The IG curve starts at (and finishes near) the random curve's final value — the zoomed panel on the right makes the small end-of-training gap legible.

    In [7]:
    Copied! 
    trained_random, losses_random = fit_to_data(
    jr.key(10),
    flow_random,
    X,
    learning_rate=5e-3,
    max_epochs=150,
    max_patience=150,
    batch_size=512,
    val_prop=0.1,
    show_progress=False,
)
trained_ig, losses_ig = fit_to_data(
    jr.key(11),
    flow_ig,
    X,
    learning_rate=5e-3,
    max_epochs=150,
    max_patience=150,
    batch_size=512,
    val_prop=0.1,
    show_progress=False,
)
rnd_curve = np.asarray(losses_random["train"])
ig_curve = np.asarray(losses_ig["train"])

fig, axes = plt.subplots(1, 2, figsize=(17, 6.5))

ax = axes[0]
ax.plot(rnd_curve, label="random init", color=COLOR_RANDOM, linewidth=2.2)
ax.plot(ig_curve, label="IG init", color=COLOR_IG, linewidth=2.2)
ax.set_xlabel("epoch")
ax.set_ylabel(r"training loss  $(-\log p_X + \text{const})$")
ax.set_title("Diagonal flow — full")
ax.legend(frameon=True)
style_axes(ax)

ax = axes[1]
tail_start = 15
tail_rnd = rnd_curve[tail_start:]
tail_ig = ig_curve[tail_start:]
both = np.concatenate([tail_rnd, tail_ig])
span = both.max() - both.min()
ax.plot(
    range(tail_start, len(rnd_curve)),
    tail_rnd,
    label="random init",
    color=COLOR_RANDOM,
    linewidth=2.2,
)
ax.plot(
    range(tail_start, len(ig_curve)),
    tail_ig,
    label="IG init",
    color=COLOR_IG,
    linewidth=2.2,
)
ax.set_ylim(both.min() - 0.05 * span, both.max() + 0.05 * span)
ax.set_xlabel("epoch")
ax.set_ylabel("loss")
ax.set_title(rf"Zoomed  (epochs $\geq$ {tail_start})")
ax.legend(frameon=True)
style_axes(ax)
plt.show()
print(
    f"final loss:  random init = {rnd_curve[-1]:+.3f}   IG init = {ig_curve[-1]:+.3f}"
)
    trained_random, losses_random = fit_to_data( jr.key(10), flow_random, X, learning_rate=5e-3, max_epochs=150, max_patience=150, batch_size=512, val_prop=0.1, show_progress=False, ) trained_ig, losses_ig = fit_to_data( jr.key(11), flow_ig, X, learning_rate=5e-3, max_epochs=150, max_patience=150, batch_size=512, val_prop=0.1, show_progress=False, ) rnd_curve = np.asarray(losses_random["train"]) ig_curve = np.asarray(losses_ig["train"]) fig, axes = plt.subplots(1, 2, figsize=(17, 6.5)) ax = axes[0] ax.plot(rnd_curve, label="random init", color=COLOR_RANDOM, linewidth=2.2) ax.plot(ig_curve, label="IG init", color=COLOR_IG, linewidth=2.2) ax.set_xlabel("epoch") ax.set_ylabel(r"training loss $(-\log p_X + \text{const})$") ax.set_title("Diagonal flow — full") ax.legend(frameon=True) style_axes(ax) ax = axes[1] tail_start = 15 tail_rnd = rnd_curve[tail_start:] tail_ig = ig_curve[tail_start:] both = np.concatenate([tail_rnd, tail_ig]) span = both.max() - both.min() ax.plot( range(tail_start, len(rnd_curve)), tail_rnd, label="random init", color=COLOR_RANDOM, linewidth=2.2, ) ax.plot( range(tail_start, len(ig_curve)), tail_ig, label="IG init", color=COLOR_IG, linewidth=2.2, ) ax.set_ylim(both.min() - 0.05 * span, both.max() + 0.05 * span) ax.set_xlabel("epoch") ax.set_ylabel("loss") ax.set_title(rf"Zoomed (epochs $\geq$ {tail_start})") ax.legend(frameon=True) style_axes(ax) plt.show() print( f"final loss: random init = {rnd_curve[-1]:+.3f} IG init = {ig_curve[-1]:+.3f}" )

    Density and samples after training¶

    In [8]:
    Copied! 
    grid = 220
xs = np.linspace(-2.5, 2.5, grid).astype("float32")
ys = np.linspace(-2.5, 2.5, grid).astype("float32")
xx, yy = np.meshgrid(xs, ys)
pts = np.stack([xx.ravel(), yy.ravel()], axis=-1).astype("float32")

log_px_rnd = np.asarray(jax.vmap(trained_random.log_prob)(jnp.asarray(pts))).reshape(
    grid, grid
)
log_px_ig = np.asarray(jax.vmap(trained_ig.log_prob)(jnp.asarray(pts))).reshape(
    grid, grid
)

fig, axes = plt.subplots(1, 2, figsize=(17, 7.5))
for ax, lp, title in zip(
    axes, [log_px_rnd, log_px_ig], ["Random init — density", "IG init — density"]
):
    pcm = ax.pcolormesh(xx, yy, np.exp(lp), cmap="magma", shading="auto")
    ax.scatter(
        np.asarray(X[:800, 0]), np.asarray(X[:800, 1]), s=2, alpha=0.25, color="white"
    )
    ax.set_title(title)
    ax.set_xlabel("$x_1$")
    ax.set_ylabel("$x_2$")
    style_axes(ax, aspect="equal")
    fig.colorbar(pcm, ax=ax, shrink=0.85)
plt.show()

samples_rnd = np.asarray(trained_random.sample(jr.key(2), (3000,)))
samples_ig = np.asarray(trained_ig.sample(jr.key(2), (3000,)))

for s, title, col in [
    (samples_rnd, "Random init — samples", COLOR_RANDOM),
    (samples_ig, "IG init — samples", COLOR_IG),
]:
    g = sns.jointplot(
        x=s[:, 0],
        y=s[:, 1],
        kind="scatter",
        color=col,
        height=7.5,
        ratio=5,
        space=0.1,
        joint_kws={"s": 10, "alpha": 0.55},
        marginal_kws={"bins": 50, "color": col, "alpha": 0.75, "edgecolor": "white"},
        xlim=(-2.5, 2.5),
        ylim=(-2.5, 2.5),
    )

    3. Coupling flow — random vs IG init¶

    Same experiment with a coupling flow. IG init for coupling layers is weaker in isolation (the conditioner is not exercised at init — it emits a constant bias), but it still lets training skip the "the conditioner is effectively random, so the coupling transform is random" phase by handing it a sensible starting point where the conditioner behaves as a well-fit diagonal marginal.

    In [9]:
    Copied! 
    N_BLOCKS_CPL = 4
NN_WIDTH = 64
NN_DEPTH = 2


def _build_random_coupling_flow(key, n_blocks, n_components):
    """Build a MixtureGaussianCDFCoupling flow with the same architecture as
    ``fit_rbig_coupling`` but random init (no IG warm-start)."""

    def make_block(k):
        rk, ck1, ck2 = jr.split(k, 3)
        rot = HouseholderRotation(n_reflections=2, shape=(2,))
        rot = eqx.tree_at(lambda r: r.params, rot, jr.normal(rk, rot.params.shape))
        c1 = MixtureGaussianCDFCoupling(
            ck1,
            shape=(2,),
            n_components=n_components,
            nn_width=NN_WIDTH,
            nn_depth=NN_DEPTH,
        )
        c2 = MixtureGaussianCDFCoupling(
            ck2,
            shape=(2,),
            n_components=n_components,
            nn_width=NN_WIDTH,
            nn_depth=NN_DEPTH,
        )
        flip = Flip(shape=(2,))
        return Chain([rot, c1, flip, c2, flip])

    blocks = eqx.filter_vmap(make_block)(jr.split(key, n_blocks))
    bijection = Invert(Scan(blocks))
    return Transformed(Normal(jnp.zeros(2)), bijection)


cpl_random = _build_random_coupling_flow(
    jr.key(3), n_blocks=N_BLOCKS_CPL, n_components=N_COMPONENTS
)
cpl_ig = fit_rbig_coupling(
    X,
    jr.key(3),
    n_layers=N_BLOCKS_CPL,
    n_components=N_COMPONENTS,
    nn_width=NN_WIDTH,
    nn_depth=NN_DEPTH,
)

lp_crnd0 = float(jax.vmap(cpl_random.log_prob)(X).mean())
lp_cig0 = float(jax.vmap(cpl_ig.log_prob)(X).mean())
print("mean log-likelihood before training (coupling flow):")
print(f"  random init : {lp_crnd0:+.3f} nats/sample")
print(
    f"  IG init     : {lp_cig0:+.3f} nats/sample  "
    f"(improvement: {lp_cig0 - lp_crnd0:+.3f})"
)

    4. Verifying the zero-kernel contract¶

    Immediately after fit_rbig_coupling every MixtureGaussianCDFCoupling's final Dense has a zero kernel (so the conditioner emits its bias for any input — the coupling layer behaves as a diagonal marginal on its b-half). During gradient training those kernels become non-zero as the conditioner learns to modulate on $x_a$. Below: build a fresh coupling flow, IG-init it, check the kernels before any training, then train briefly and check again. Notebook 04 proves the full-flow equivalence.

    In [13]:
    Copied! 
    def max_final_kernel(flow):
    """Return max|W| of every coupling's conditioner final Dense."""
    out = []
    chain = flow.bijection.bijection  # Invert → Chain
    for bij in chain.bijections:
        if isinstance(bij, _CouplingClass):
            final = bij._coupling.conditioner.layers[-1]
            out.append(float(jnp.max(jnp.abs(final.weight))))
    return out


cpl_probe = fit_rbig_coupling(
    X,
    jr.key(42),
    n_layers=N_BLOCKS_CPL,
    n_components=N_COMPONENTS,
    nn_width=NN_WIDTH,
    nn_depth=NN_DEPTH,
)
kernels_post_ig = max_final_kernel(cpl_probe)
print(
    f"right after IG init (no train):   max|W| per coupling = "
    f"{[f'{k:.1e}' for k in kernels_post_ig]}"
)
print(f"all zero after IG init : {all(k < 1e-6 for k in kernels_post_ig)}")

probe_trained, _ = fit_to_data(
    jr.key(43),
    cpl_probe,
    X,
    learning_rate=3e-3,
    max_epochs=20,
    max_patience=20,
    batch_size=512,
    val_prop=0.1,
    show_progress=False,
)
kernels_after_train = max_final_kernel(probe_trained)
print(
    f"after 20 epochs of training:      max|W| per coupling = "
    f"{[f'{k:.3f}' for k in kernels_after_train]}"
)
print("(non-zero is expected — the conditioner has started to modulate on x_a)")

    Recap¶

    • RBIG (Laparra & Malo 2011) is a non-gradient greedy warm-start that fits each block's parameters in sequence (PCA for rotation, sklearn GaussianMixture per dim for marginal/coupling) and propagates the data forward.
    • For the diagonal flow the init is exact: the layer's $(\pi, \mu, \sigma)$ parameters are exactly the GMM fit, and the pre-training pushforward is already near $\mathcal{N}(0, I)$.
    • For the coupling flow the conditioner's inner Dense weights stay random, but the final Dense is forced to kernel=0, bias = fitted mixture params. So at init the coupling layer behaves like a diagonal marginal layer with the IG-fitted mixture; gradient training then lets the conditioner become genuinely conditional.
    • End result in both cases: lower starting NLL, faster convergence, and fewer chances for the optimiser to get stuck in a bad local minimum.
    Made with Material for MkDocs
